Let me analyze this question based on my knowledge of chemistry and crystallography:

A. Assessing the folding extent of a Zn2Cl2 four-membered ring - X-ray crystallography can determine the three-dimensional structure of molecules, including ring conformations. It can measure bond lengths, angles, and the spatial arrangement of atoms, so it can assess folding in a four-membered ring.

B. Determining the Si-O-Si bond angle in a mineral - X-ray crystallography can measure bond angles in crystalline structures, including minerals. This is one of the primary applications of X-ray crystallography.

C. Establishing the absolute configuration of a chiral natural product - X-ray crystallography can determine absolute configurations of chiral molecules, especially when heavy atoms are present or with modern techniques like anomalous dispersion.

D. Identifying the vibration frequency of a carbonyl group - X-ray crystallography provides a static picture of molecular structure. It doesn't measure molecular vibrations or frequencies. Vibration frequencies are typically measured using spectroscopic techniques like infrared (IR) spectroscopy or Raman spectroscopy, not X-ray crystallography.

Based on this analysis, the information that cannot be obtained through X-ray crystallography is the vibration frequency of a carbonyl group.
